title: Steelers vs. Eagles? In 1943 They Were the Same Team
description:
The Steelers and Eagles are in the news this week, but in 1943 they weren't rivals: World War II left both clubs so short of players that they merged into one team, officially the "Phil-Pitt Combine" and, to everyone else, the Steagles. Here's how that one wartime season went.

Every frame is drawn with code. No stock footage, no AI video.

Note: Figures follow the Pro Football Hall of Fame, the Philadelphia Eagles' "The Year They Were One" (Ray Didinger), the Philadelphia Inquirer and CBS Sports. About 600 NFL players served in the armed forces during the war; the Steelers had six players under contract and the Eagles sixteen (some accounts give a lower Eagles count). The league's record book lists the team as the Phil-Pitt Combine; "Steagles" was a newspaper nickname. Co-coaches Greasy Neale and Walt Kiesling are reported not to have gotten along. The receiver blind in one eye was Tony Bova. The 1943 team went 5-4-1, the first winning season in Eagles history; in 1944 Pittsburgh merged with the Chicago Cardinals ("Card-Pitt") and went winless. The 1920s football photos and the 1914 Philadelphia photo show the era and the city, not the 1943 team itself.

Images (public domain): game photographs, Yale and Harvard 1920-21, from Percy D. Haughton, "Football and How to Watch It" (1922, Internet Archive); "Watching World's Series game, Phila." 1914, Bain News Service (Library of Congress); U.S. infantry in France, 1944, U.S. Army Signal Corps (NARA); "We Can Do It!" by J. Howard Miller for Westinghouse, 1943 (NARA 535413). Documents and the selective service classification drawn in code.
Maps drawn in code from Natural Earth (world-atlas) and US Census (us-atlas) outlines.
Narration voice is synthetic.
